reviewBoundary: All chapters in this batch are technical-review drafts. They are not verified production instructions and contain no universal machine or material setpoints.

sourceSeeds.title: Plastics — Injection moulding of test specimens of thermoplastic materials — Part 4: Determination of moulding shrinkage
sourceSeeds.scope: Method for moulding and post-moulding shrinkage of thermoplastic test specimens; ISO confirmed this edition in 2024.

sourceSeeds.title: Plastics moulded parts — Tolerances and acceptance conditions
sourceSeeds.scope: Current 2026 plastics-specific dimensional/geometrical tolerance and acceptance framework; identifies material, moulding shrinkage, processing conditions, geometry, cooling and warpage as dimensional influences.

sourceSeeds.title: Standard Test Method of Measuring Shrinkage from Mold Dimensions of Thermoplastics
sourceSeeds.scope: Thermoplastic moulding shrinkage test method; explicitly notes effects of mould/melt temperature, fill time and packing and limits extrapolation from standard specimens to production parts.

chapters.applicability: General thermoplastic reciprocating-screw moulding. Transfer methods and signal quality depend on the machine, mould and instrumentation.

sections.title: What transfer means
sections.text: Velocity-to-pressure transfer changes the dominant control objective from advancing the screw to filling the cavity toward controlling post-fill pressure. The useful transfer point is therefore a process boundary, not a universal screw-position percentage.

sections.title: Why timing matters
sections.text: Transfer too early can leave the cavity under-filled before packing; transfer too late can create a sharp pressure rise, over-packing, flash or unnecessary load. Those outcomes are hypotheses to confirm from part response and process signals.

sections.title: How to establish it
sections.text: Use a controlled fill study, repeatable melt preparation and the actual machine's transfer options. Record screw position, time and pressure behavior, and verify that the chosen method remains stable across normal process variation.

sections.title: Transfer is a control transition, not a universal percentage
sections.text: The useful transfer point is the point at which the process should stop being governed primarily by filling motion and begin controlling the post-fill response. Position, pressure, time or cavity-based methods can all be meaningful in the right system, but a copied percentage has no universal authority. Evaluate repeatability, cavity response, part mass and defect behaviour while preserving machine and mould limits.

sections.title: Look for evidence of early or late transfer
sections.text: A transfer that occurs too early for the actual process can leave the cavity dependent on post-transfer filling, while a transfer that occurs too late can create excessive pressure response or overfill tendencies. Interpret the evidence as a pattern across position, pressure, time, cavity behaviour and part results rather than declaring one trace feature to be proof by itself.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Conceptual relationship only. Required clamp capability depends on projected area, cavity pressure distribution, mould construction and machine limits.

sections.title: What clamp force resists
sections.text: Melt pressure acting over the projected area tends to separate the mould halves. The clamp system must resist opening while the mould and machine remain within their rated limits.

sections.title: Why a single formula is not enough
sections.text: Projected area and an assumed pressure can provide an engineering estimate, but local cavity pressure, runner area, cavity count, mould stiffness and machine behavior affect the real requirement.

sections.title: Mould protection is different
sections.text: Low-force mould-protection functions are intended to detect abnormal resistance during closing; they are not a substitute for correct tooling, guarding, maintenance or the machine manufacturer's setup procedure.

sections.title: Clamp demand is a distributed-pressure problem
sections.text: The mould-opening tendency depends on pressure acting over projected areas, but cavity pressure is not uniform in space or time and machine injection pressure is not a direct substitute for the pressure distribution at the parting line. Clamp calculations are therefore engineering estimates whose assumptions should be visible. They can support machine and process decisions, but they do not automatically define the required machine rating.

sections.title: Flash is not automatically a clamp-tonnage diagnosis
sections.text: Flash can involve clamp force, pressure, mould damage, parting-line contamination, local support, temperature, viscosity, vent geometry or other mechanisms. Increasing clamp force without evidence can hide tooling issues or move the process toward equipment limits. Check where flash occurs, whether it is cavity-specific, how it changes with pressure history and whether the mould closes and supports correctly before naming the cause.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General cold- and hot-feed-system concepts; actual dimensions and limits are mould-specific.

sections.title: Flow path
sections.text: The feed system carries melt from the machine nozzle to the cavity. Its restrictions consume pressure and influence shear, temperature history and balance.

sections.title: Gates are process boundaries
sections.text: Gate geometry controls how the cavity is fed and how long post-fill pressure can influence the part. Changing a gate can alter filling, packing, orientation and appearance together.

sections.title: Diagnose by location
sections.text: When a restriction is suspected, separate machine/nozzle, sprue, runner, gate and cavity contributions using measured or controlled comparisons rather than assuming the smallest feature is automatically the root cause.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General mechanism guidance. Vent geometry, cleaning and permissible modification are mould- and material-specific.

sections.title: Air must leave
sections.text: As melt advances, displaced air and process gases need escape paths. If gas is trapped or compressed faster than it can leave, filling behavior and surface quality can deteriorate.

sections.title: Burns are not one mechanism
sections.text: A dark mark near an end-of-fill region can be consistent with compressed gas, but thermal degradation, contamination and excessive residence history can produce similar evidence.

sections.title: Test before changing steel
sections.text: Use defect location, fill progression, vent condition and controlled process changes to test the hypothesis. Permanent vent changes require tooling authority and mould-specific limits.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Heat-transfer principles only. Coolant, flow, pressure, mould materials and allowable temperatures are tool- and site-specific.

sections.title: Cooling drives repeatability
sections.text: The mould removes heat from the polymer and establishes the thermal boundary conditions from cycle to cycle. Uneven heat removal can create local differences in shrinkage, stiffness at ejection and warpage.

sections.title: Setpoint is not surface temperature
sections.text: A temperature-control-unit setpoint does not prove the temperature of every cavity surface. Circuit layout, flow, fouling and local heat load can produce differences.

sections.title: Measure the system
sections.text: Evaluate stable cycle time, coolant supply/return behavior where available, mould-surface temperature with an appropriate method, and part response before attributing variation to cooling generically.

sections.title: Cooling governs both cycle readiness and dimensional state
sections.text: The cooling stage removes heat non-uniformly from a three-dimensional part and mould. Local wall thickness, coolant layout, mould material, contact, crystallisation where applicable and part geometry can create different temperature histories across the component. Ejection readiness and later dimensions therefore depend on more than one timer value.

sections.title: Diagnose the thermal system with trends, not one reading
sections.text: Useful evidence can include coolant supply and return conditions, mould-surface measurements, cycle-to-cycle warm-up behaviour, cavity pattern, part temperature and dimensional change after ejection. A single temperature measurement may miss an imbalance. Look for spatial and time patterns that distinguish a stable offset from changing heat load, restricted flow, poor contact or another thermal mechanism.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General release mechanisms. Draft requirements and ejection limits depend on geometry, texture, material and tool construction.

sections.title: Release is mechanical and thermal
sections.text: The moulded part contracts and may grip cores or features as it cools. Draft, surface texture, geometry and local stiffness affect the force needed for release.

sections.title: Ejection evidence matters
sections.text: Drag marks, whitening, distortion or pin witness can indicate excessive release load, but the cause may be insufficient cooling, poor draft, local undercut, surface damage or pressure history.

sections.title: Do not cure tooling problems blindly
sections.text: Process changes can alter release forces, but persistent mechanical interference or inadequate draft should be evaluated as tooling/design conditions rather than hidden with unsafe or unstable settings.

sections.title: Release force carries information
sections.text: Ejection marks, distortion, sticking and changing ejector load can reflect part temperature, shrinkage onto cores, surface condition, draft, texture, vacuum effects, mould contamination or mechanical alignment. Treat release behaviour as evidence about the part-mould interface rather than automatically increasing ejection force or cooling time.

sections.title: Separate geometry from process effects
sections.text: If a release problem follows one feature or cavity consistently, geometry, finish, venting or local cooling deserves attention. If it drifts with mould temperature or cycle state, process and thermal mechanisms become more plausible. Controlled comparisons help avoid using process compensation to mask a tooling condition that requires inspection or repair.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General hot-runner concepts only. Temperatures, start-up, shutdown, maintenance and valve-gate timing must follow the installed supplier's documentation.

sections.title: A heated feed system is part of the process
sections.text: Hot runners keep material molten in some or all of the feed path, reducing cold-runner solidification but adding thermal zones, flow restrictions and control elements.

sections.title: Thermal history can differ by location
sections.text: Manifold and nozzle temperatures, residence distribution and local restrictions can affect viscosity and degradation risk. A controller setpoint alone does not prove melt condition.

sections.title: Supplier instructions control
sections.text: Start-up, shutdown, purge, heater limits, valve-gate operation and maintenance are hardware- and material-dependent. Generic Book guidance cannot safely replace the hot-runner supplier's procedure.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Framework for documenting a stable starting condition; not a recipe for selecting material-specific setpoints.

sections.title: Start inside known limits
sections.text: Confirm the material identity and preparation, machine and mould condition, and controlling supplier/site requirements before optimization.

sections.title: Record what can reproduce the state
sections.text: Capture relevant temperatures, positions, velocities, pressures, times, material lot/condition, mould temperature information and observed part results using consistent units.

sections.title: Stability before optimization
sections.text: Allow the process to reach a repeatable thermal and mechanical condition before judging small changes. A moving baseline makes cause-and-effect conclusions unreliable.

sections.title: A baseline records state, not just setpoints
sections.text: A defensible baseline includes the material identity and condition, machine and mould identity, relevant controller settings, measured process responses, thermal state, cavity or part measurements and the timing of the observation. Setpoints alone are incomplete because they do not prove what the machine, melt or cavity actually did.

sections.title: Baseline before optimisation
sections.text: When a process is changing from cycle to cycle, optimisation results are difficult to interpret because the reference state is moving. Establish a repeatable baseline first, define what variation is normal, and then make controlled changes tied to measurable responses. This makes later troubleshooting faster because there is a credible comparison state rather than only operator memory.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Experimental method; exact procedure and stopping criteria depend on machine, mould and material.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.text: A fill study deliberately separates cavity filling from later packing effects so the engineer can observe how the flow front progresses under controlled conditions.

sections.title: Control the comparison
sections.text: Keep material preparation, melt condition, mould thermal condition and injection profile consistent while changing the selected fill endpoint or shot contribution.

sections.title: Interpret cautiously
sections.text: Part weight, visual fill pattern, screw position and pressure traces can reveal trends, but none alone proves cavity pressure or gate behavior without appropriate measurement.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic study framework; measured pressures and safe limits are machine- and mould-specific.

sections.title: Every restriction consumes pressure
sections.text: Pressure is required to move melt through the nozzle, sprue, runners, gates and cavity. The amount depends on geometry, flow rate, material rheology and thermal condition.

sections.title: Segment the path
sections.text: Compare controlled states that add successive portions of the flow path, or use appropriately located sensors, to identify where pressure demand increases.

sections.title: Do not equate machine pressure with cavity pressure
sections.text: Displayed injection pressure is upstream of multiple restrictions. Use it as one signal in a pressure-loss analysis, not as a direct substitute for pressure inside the cavity.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Experimental determination for a specific material, gate and mould. No universal hold time applies.

sections.title: Why gate state matters
sections.text: Post-fill pressure can influence the cavity only while the feed path remains capable of transmitting material or pressure effectively.

sections.title: Use part response
sections.text: A common experimental approach is to vary hold duration under controlled conditions and observe whether a stable response such as part mass or a critical dimension reaches a plateau.

sections.title: Plateau is evidence, not a universal constant
sections.text: The result is specific to gate geometry, material, thermal state and process. Changes to those conditions can change the effective seal behavior.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Statistical/experimental concept. Acceptable limits must be tied to product requirements and equipment/material constraints.

sections.title: A setting is not a process window
sections.text: A robust process has a region in which normal input variation still produces acceptable outputs, rather than one preferred nominal point.

sections.title: Define outputs first
sections.text: Use measurable part requirements and process signals to determine what acceptable means. Cosmetic acceptance alone may miss dimensional or functional changes.

sections.title: Challenge the edges deliberately
sections.text: Controlled experiments can explore sensitivity to important variables, but only inside safe machine, mould and material limits. Document the tested region instead of claiming untested robustness.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General documentation framework; regulated products and site quality systems may require additional records.

sections.title: Record the conditions that matter
sections.text: A defensible process record identifies material, machine, mould, key process parameters, units, relevant environmental or preparation conditions, and the measured part result.

sections.title: Preserve context
sections.text: Controller names and raw setpoints can be ambiguous across machines. Record what a parameter represents, where it was measured, and any conversions or assumptions.

sections.title: Link changes to evidence
sections.text: When a process changes, record why, what evidence supported the change, and what output confirmed or rejected the hypothesis.

sections.title: Record the reasoning, not only the final setting
sections.text: A useful engineering record captures the problem statement, observations, hypothesis, controlled change, expected outcome, actual result and decision. Recording only the final parameter values loses the evidence needed to understand why the change was made or whether it remains appropriate after material, mould, machine or product changes.

sections.title: Make records comparable over time
sections.text: Use stable names, units, cavity identifiers, measurement methods and version references so records from different shifts or maintenance states can be compared. Where controlled documents or quality systems apply, preserve revision and approval boundaries. A complete checkbox without traceable evidence is weaker than a concise record that shows what was observed and why the conclusion was reached.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General troubleshooting method; safety and product-disposition decisions remain under site procedures.

sections.title: Start with the symptom
sections.text: Define the defect by location, frequency, cavity, time pattern and measurable severity before changing settings.

sections.title: Build competing mechanisms
sections.text: List plausible mechanisms involving material, machine, mould, process and measurement. Treat each as a hypothesis, not a verdict.

sections.title: Change to learn
sections.text: Choose the safest discriminating observation or controlled test, change one justified factor where practical, and use the result to update the diagnosis.

sections.title: Start with the symptom boundary
sections.text: Define exactly what is wrong before changing the process: where the symptom appears, when it began, which cavities or lots are affected, how often it occurs and how it is measured. A broad label such as 'short shot' or 'warpage' is not yet a diagnosis. The boundary of the symptom often removes whole classes of possible causes.

sections.title: Write competing mechanisms and predicted evidence
sections.text: List the plausible mechanisms that fit the observation and state what should also be true for each one. Then choose the smallest safe measurement or controlled comparison that would make those predictions diverge. This turns troubleshooting from trial-and-error adjustment into evidence generation.

sections.title: Verify recovery and guard against coincidence
sections.text: A part improving after a change is useful evidence but does not automatically prove root cause. Confirm the effect is repeatable, that the predicted process signal or boundary also changed, and that the improvement survives normal process variation. If the evidence does not discriminate between plausible causes, retain the uncertainty.

sections.title: Use chronology to reduce the search space
sections.text: Ask what changed before the symptom appeared: material lot, drying history, colour change, mould maintenance, machine change, start-up state, ambient condition, operator sequence or production interruption. Chronology does not prove causation, but it can identify boundaries that make one mechanism more plausible than another. A symptom that appears immediately after one controlled change deserves a different first test from a symptom that drifts gradually over many hours.

sections.title: Prefer tests that can falsify a favourite explanation
sections.text: Troubleshooting becomes more reliable when a test is chosen because it could show the leading hypothesis is wrong. If the suspected cause predicts a cavity pattern, time trend or signal change, look for that pattern explicitly. A test that can only confirm what the investigator already expects has weak diagnostic value. Good engineering preserves the possibility of being wrong and updates the working model when observations fail the prediction.

sections.title: Escalate when the evidence boundary is reached
sections.text: Some problems cannot be resolved from controller data and visual inspection alone. When competing mechanisms remain plausible, escalate to evidence capable of separating them: tooling inspection, material testing, cavity sensing, metrology, microscopy, maintenance history, supplier support or validated simulation. The correct outcome of a disciplined investigation can be 'not yet distinguished' rather than a falsely precise root-cause statement.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses for incomplete filling; actual corrective action depends on the identified restriction and equipment limits.

sections.title: What it tells you
sections.text: A short shot means the cavity did not receive enough effective flow to reproduce the intended geometry. It does not identify why.

sections.title: Mechanisms to distinguish
sections.text: Possible mechanisms include insufficient delivered material, premature transfer, inadequate flow capability, excessive restriction, loss of venting effectiveness, material/melt condition or machine delivery problems.

sections.title: Use evidence
sections.text: Check repeatability, screw/cushion behavior, fill pattern, pressure demand, material preparation and the physical flow path before increasing pressure or temperature indiscriminately.

sections.title: Locate where filling stops
sections.text: The position of the unfilled region can indicate whether the issue is global filling capacity, local flow resistance, venting, premature freezing, cavity imbalance or an intermittent delivery problem. Compare fill pattern across cavities and over time before assuming that simply increasing pressure, speed or material temperature is the correct response.

sections.title: Separate command limits from delivered process
sections.text: Check whether the machine actually reached the commanded velocity, position and pressure behaviour and whether transfer or protection limits intervened. A short shot can occur even with apparently generous setpoints if the effective shot, flow path, material state or machine delivery differs from the assumption. Measured response is therefore more informative than the setting alone.

sections.title: Separate repeatable shortage from intermittent loss
sections.text: A consistently unfilled region can indicate a stable restriction, thermal condition, shot-delivery limit or venting problem. An intermittent short shot can point toward inconsistent check-valve behaviour, material feed, transfer repeatability, air, machine delivery or changing mould conditions. Time-order the events rather than pooling good and bad cycles; intermittency itself is evidence about the mechanism.

sections.title: Use cavity comparison in multi-cavity moulds
sections.text: When only one cavity shorts, compare that cavity's runner or gate path, venting, thermal condition and local filling evidence with the others. When every cavity degrades together, upstream material or machine effects become more plausible. A global setting change may temporarily fill the weak cavity while overdriving the others, so cavity-resolved evidence should precede permanent compensation.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses only. Never exceed machine or mould limits to suppress or create flash.

sections.title: What flash means
sections.text: Flash is material outside the intended cavity boundary. It can occur when local melt pressure opens or enters a gap large enough for the material under the actual thermal and rheological condition.

sections.title: Competing causes
sections.text: Tool damage or mismatch, inadequate clamping condition, excessive cavity pressure, over-packing, low melt viscosity and contamination at shutoff surfaces can produce similar symptoms.

sections.title: Locate before correcting
sections.text: Map where flash occurs and when it appeared. Separate tooling condition from process pressure history instead of assuming more clamp force is always the answer.

sections.title: Map flash before changing clamp or pressure
sections.text: Flash around the whole parting line suggests a different investigation from flash at one insert, vent, slide or cavity. Record location, thickness, timing and cavity identity. A local pattern can indicate tooling support, damage, contamination or vent geometry, while a process-wide pattern may support a different mechanism.

sections.title: Treat process compensation as evidence, not proof
sections.text: If a pressure or temperature change reduces flash, that shows the defect responds to the process state but does not prove the mould is healthy or identify the root cause. Verify whether the corrected condition remains inside the qualified process window and whether tooling inspection is warranted before institutionalising compensation.

sections.title: Parting-line support and local pressure matter
sections.text: A mould can experience local opening or material escape even when the nominal machine clamp setting appears adequate. Local geometry, support, wear, contamination and pressure distribution influence what happens at a specific region. Because pressure falls through the flow path and varies with time, a machine pressure display cannot by itself establish the local force acting where flash appears.

sections.title: Verify the fix does not create a new defect
sections.text: A change that removes flash can also alter fill balance, packing, dimensions, residual stress or mould protection margin. Re-check the product characteristics and process signals that matter after any corrective trial. A defensible fix should restore the intended boundary without merely moving the process to another edge of its operating window.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Mechanism guidance for thermoplastic parts; acceptance and correction depend on geometry, material and product requirements.

sections.title: Both arise from contraction
sections.text: As polymer cools, volume changes. Thick or thermally isolated regions can continue contracting after the surface has stiffened.

sections.title: Surface sink and internal void are different outcomes
sections.text: If the surface can move inward, a depression can form; if the outer shell resists that movement, an internal void can develop. Geometry and pressure transmission influence which outcome dominates.

sections.title: Test the pressure-and-cooling history
sections.text: Evaluate gate effectiveness, packing response, local wall/thickness transitions and cooling before applying generic pressure or time increases.

sections.title: Sink and internal voids are related but not identical
sections.text: Both can arise when volumetric contraction is not adequately accommodated, but the visible or internal result depends on geometry, pressure transmission, gate isolation, material behaviour and cooling. External sink, internal voiding and acceptable surface with hidden porosity can therefore require different measurements even when they share part of the same physical story.

sections.title: Use section location and time response
sections.text: Map the defect against thick sections, ribs, bosses, gate distance and cooling features. Then compare the response to controlled packing and cooling changes within safe limits. If additional post-fill pressure no longer affects the region, the feed path may no longer transmit useful pressure; that is a different conclusion from assuming more hold time is always beneficial.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic framework. Moisture limits and drying conditions are grade-specific.

sections.title: Appearance is not a unique diagnosis
sections.text: Silver streaks or splay can be associated with moisture or other volatiles, but air entrainment, contamination and thermal degradation can create similar visual evidence.

sections.title: Material evidence first
sections.text: Confirm material identity, storage history and the grade supplier's drying/moisture requirements using suitable measurement where required.

sections.title: Avoid over-drying by guesswork
sections.text: Drying hotter or longer is not universally safer; excessive thermal exposure can also damage some materials. Follow grade-specific documentation.

sections.title: Splay is an appearance, not a root cause
sections.text: Silver or streaked surface patterns can be consistent with moisture, other volatiles, air entrainment, decompression effects, contamination or degradation. Use location, material history, lot pattern, dryer evidence, residence history and process timing to discriminate among mechanisms. Avoid converting a familiar visual pattern into an automatic drying diagnosis.

sections.title: Ask what should change if the hypothesis is true
sections.text: A moisture hypothesis predicts a relationship with verified material condition; a degradation hypothesis predicts a relationship with thermal history; an air-entrapment hypothesis may follow geometry or decompression conditions. Controlled evidence that separates these predictions is stronger than repeated parameter changes that all alter the appearance.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses for dark/burned areas; purge and intervention procedures remain machine/site specific.

sections.title: Separate gas compression from degradation
sections.text: End-of-fill burns can be consistent with trapped compressed gas, while dark degraded material may originate from excessive thermal history, dead spots or contamination.

sections.title: Location and timing discriminate
sections.text: A repeatable mark at a trapped-air location suggests a different investigation from intermittent black material appearing across cavities or after stoppages.

sections.title: Correct the mechanism
sections.text: Investigate venting and fill behavior for gas compression; investigate residence history, temperatures, material compatibility and flow dead zones for degradation.

sections.title: Distinguish compressed gas from thermal degradation
sections.text: Dark or scorched marks near end-of-fill regions can be consistent with trapped gas heating, while degraded material can also create dark contamination. Location, vent condition, fill pattern, residence history and whether the mark follows the mould or material path help distinguish the mechanisms. The visual symptom alone is insufficient.

sections.title: Vent work is tooling work
sections.text: When evidence points toward restricted venting, inspection or modification must follow approved tooling and safety procedures. Generic teaching can explain why gas escape matters and how a pattern may support the hypothesis; it cannot prescribe unreviewed vent dimensions or authorise cutting steel.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General flow-front mechanism; strength/appearance impact depends on material, geometry and product requirement.

sections.title: How they form
sections.text: A weld or knit region forms where separate melt fronts meet after flowing around an obstacle or from different gates.

sections.title: Quality depends on the meeting conditions
sections.text: Temperature, pressure, contamination, trapped gas, orientation and the angle/time of flow-front meeting can affect how well the interface develops.

sections.title: Treat location as a design-process interaction
sections.text: Moving or strengthening a weld region may involve gate strategy, geometry, venting, material and process changes; no single temperature increase is a universal fix.

sections.title: A weld line records a flow-front meeting event
sections.text: Weld or knit lines form where separate melt fronts meet after flowing around features, through multiple gates or across interrupted paths. Their appearance and strength can depend on local temperature, pressure, orientation, contamination, venting and geometry. The line is therefore a process-and-design interaction, not merely a cosmetic mark.

sections.title: Evaluate both location and performance
sections.text: Moving or visually reducing a weld line is not automatically an improvement if structural performance matters. Record where the fronts meet, whether gas must escape there, what load direction the product experiences and how the relevant quality characteristic is measured. Process changes should be judged against that product requirement rather than appearance alone.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Revise the working explanation when the line location does not follow expected flow-front changes, when strength does not track appearance, or when cavity and vent patterns contradict the assumed mechanism. Escalate to design, tooling, material or simulation evidence where process observations cannot discriminate the cause.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General mechanism and measurement framework. Prediction requires actual material, geometry, mould and process data.

sections.title: Warpage is differential deformation
sections.text: Warpage occurs when different regions or directions of a moulded part do not contract or relax by the same amount. The visible shape error is therefore an outcome of differential shrinkage, residual stress, anisotropy and constraint rather than a single setting being universally too high or too low.

sections.title: Build a mechanism map before changing the process
sections.text: Separate plausible contributors into material, flow/orientation, packing, mould thermal balance, cooling geometry, wall-thickness distribution, ejection restraint and post-mould conditioning. More than one mechanism can act at the same time, and correcting one may expose another.

sections.title: Measure shape, direction and time
sections.text: Define datum strategy, measurement method, conditioning state, time after moulding and the direction/magnitude of deformation. A part measured hot, immediately after ejection or after moisture conditioning is not automatically comparable with a part measured under a different reference condition.

sections.title: Use cavity and time patterns to discriminate causes
sections.text: A repeatable bias in one cavity suggests a different investigation from a drift shared by every cavity as the mould warms. Directional deformation aligned with flow can support an orientation hypothesis, while local distortion around thick sections can support a thermal or shrinkage-gradient hypothesis. These patterns guide testing but do not prove cause by themselves.

sections.title: Change one mechanism-relevant variable at a time where practical
sections.text: Use controlled comparisons that are capable of producing different predictions for competing hypotheses. Examples include comparing cavity-specific dimensional vectors, stable mould-temperature conditions, packing response, cooling balance or conditioning time while remaining inside approved equipment, material and product limits.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Revise the diagnosis when measured deformation does not follow the predicted direction, cavity pattern, thermal trend or process response. If several mechanisms remain consistent with the observations, preserve the uncertainty and escalate to additional measurement, tooling inspection, material evidence or simulation rather than forcing a single root cause.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses. Purging, disassembly and maintenance must use approved machine/material procedures.

sections.title: What the defect suggests
sections.text: Black specks are evidence of foreign or degraded material. Possible sources include contamination, thermally degraded polymer, stagnant material, incompatible changeover residue or external debris.

sections.title: Pattern matters
sections.text: Intermittent specks after downtime suggest a different investigation from a continuous contamination stream tied to a specific raw-material container.

sections.title: Do not create a safety problem while diagnosing
sections.text: Hot purging, nozzle work and barrel intervention involve machine-specific hazards. Follow authorised procedures rather than improvised cleaning methods.

sections.title: Trace the contamination path
sections.text: Black specks can originate from degraded polymer, dead spots, previous material, contamination, hot-runner regions, screw/barrel condition or external handling. Note whether specks appear at start-up, after stoppage, continuously, in specific cavities or after a material change. The time and cavity pattern can narrow where in the material path the source is likely to exist.

sections.title: Cleaning success does not automatically prove origin
sections.text: A purge or cleaning action that reduces specks shows the defect is responsive to that intervention but may not identify the original source. Confirm whether recurrence follows residence, shutdown, hot-runner state, material handling or another boundary. Persistent recurrence deserves equipment or tooling inspection rather than an endless purge cycle.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Sensor-based process analysis. Sensor selection, installation, calibration and limits are manufacturer- and mould-specific.

sections.title: Why measure in the cavity
sections.text: A cavity sensor observes pressure closer to where the part forms than the machine injection-pressure signal, reducing ambiguity from upstream losses.

sections.title: Curve features need context
sections.text: Rise, transfer response, peak, packing decay and gate isolation can be useful signatures, but interpretation depends on sensor position, type, calibration and mould geometry.

sections.title: Use correlations carefully
sections.text: A stable relationship between a pressure feature and part quality can support monitoring; it does not automatically prove causation outside the studied process window.

sections.title: Sensor location defines what the trace means
sections.text: A cavity-pressure sensor observes pressure at its installation location, not a uniform pressure for the entire cavity. Gate distance, local geometry, sensor type and mounting influence interpretation. Compare traces at the same sensor and process state before using absolute values across different moulds or locations.

sections.title: Use the trace as evidence of sequence
sections.text: The shape and timing of a cavity-pressure trace can help show filling arrival, transfer response, post-fill pressure transmission and decay, but the trace does not name root cause by itself. Combine it with machine signals, cavity identity, part measurements and controlled process changes. The most useful interpretation explains both the signal change and the product response.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General experimental-design principles; experiment ranges must stay within safe and qualified limits.

sections.title: Why designed experiments help
sections.text: Designed experiments are useful when several controllable factors may affect the same response and interactions are plausible. A structured design can separate effects more efficiently than informal one-factor-at-a-time adjustment, but only within ranges that are safe, technically justified and relevant to the real process window.

sections.title: Start with a process question, not a software design
sections.text: State the decision the experiment must support, define measurable responses and identify the mechanisms that could plausibly affect them. Then select factors, levels, blocking variables and replicates that can discriminate among those explanations. An elegant statistical design is weak if its factors do not represent the process physics.

sections.title: Protect the experiment from nuisance variation
sections.text: Material lot or moisture state, mould thermal condition, machine warm-up, cavity identity, operator sequence, measurement timing and ambient conditions can obscure the effects being studied. Randomisation, blocking and consistent preconditioning help prevent time trends or hidden groups from being mistaken for factor effects.

sections.title: Interpret interactions explicitly
sections.text: When the effect of one factor changes depending on the level of another, a main-effect average can be misleading. Review interaction plots, residual behavior and engineering mechanism together rather than converting one coefficient or p-value into a universal rule.

sections.title: Separate statistical significance from useful engineering change
sections.text: A detectable effect may be too small to matter to the product, while an important effect can be missed when measurement noise or sample size is inadequate. Report effect size, uncertainty, response variation and product relevance alongside significance tests.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Reconsider the model when residuals show structure, repeat runs disagree, the effect disappears under confirmation trials, factor changes produce physically implausible responses, or the tested range does not represent production. Confirmation runs and mechanism-consistent predictions are required before promoting an experimental result into a process rule.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General quality-engineering concepts. Capability indices are meaningful only under their statistical assumptions and customer/site definitions.

sections.title: Stability and measurement credibility come first
sections.text: Capability indices summarize observed process performance against specification limits only when the underlying process and measurement system are sufficiently understood. A drifting mean, changing variation or weak measurement system can make a precise-looking index misleading.

sections.title: Distinguish specification, control and process behavior
sections.text: Specification limits define acceptable product requirements; control limits describe expected process behavior under a chosen statistical model. They are not interchangeable. A process can be statistically stable yet incapable, or capable over a short sample while not being stable enough for a defensible long-term claim.

sections.title: Examine the distribution instead of assuming it
sections.text: Histogram shape, subgroup behavior, time order, outliers, multiple cavities and bounded measurements can violate simple normal and independent assumptions. Where assumptions do not fit, use an appropriate method and state it rather than reporting Cp/Cpk mechanically.

sections.title: Separate cavity and time effects
sections.text: Pooling multiple cavities or long periods into one calculation can hide systematic cavity offsets, warm-up effects, tool maintenance changes or material-lot shifts. Review cavity-level and time-ordered data before deciding which population a capability statement actually represents.

sections.title: Report the evidence behind the number
sections.text: A useful capability report includes the characteristic, specification basis, sampling plan, measurement method, process state, subgrouping, data period, excluded data with justification, chosen calculation method and uncertainty or confidence information where appropriate.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Withdraw or qualify a capability claim when the process becomes unstable, the measurement system changes, cavity populations separate, the distribution model is poor, specifications are revised, or new data materially shifts the estimated performance. Capability is a maintained evidence statement, not a permanent property of the mould.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General monitoring architecture. Available signals, sampling rates and alarm actions depend on machine/controller and site quality system.

sections.title: Monitor signals tied to mechanisms
sections.text: Useful process monitoring starts from signals that have a defensible relationship to material preparation, plasticising, filling, transfer, packing, cooling, machine function or measured part quality. A signal is more valuable when a deviation has an interpretable physical meaning.

sections.title: Define the measurement chain
sections.text: Document where each signal originates, its units, sampling behavior, filtering, calibration status and any controller transformations. Machine injection pressure, hydraulic pressure, cavity pressure, screw position and derived metrics may describe different physical locations or calculations and should not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.title: Establish a representative baseline
sections.text: Build monitoring limits from a stable, qualified operating state rather than from arbitrary historical minimum and maximum values. Include normal sources of variation such as cavities, material lots and operating phases only when they belong to the population the monitoring rule is intended to represent.

sections.title: Detect drift separately from isolated events
sections.text: Single-cycle excursions, gradual thermal drift, step changes after maintenance and recurring cavity-specific patterns call for different investigations. Time plots, run rules and cavity stratification can reveal behavior that a single pass/fail limit hides.

sections.title: Connect alarms to predefined actions
sections.text: An alarm should lead to a defined response such as verification, segregation, additional measurement or authorised process investigation. Alarm presence alone does not establish root cause, product nonconformance or the correct corrective action.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Revisit monitoring logic when alarms do not correspond to meaningful process or product changes, significant defects occur without signal movement, sensor behavior changes, or a new process state shifts the normal population. Monitoring models require maintenance just as the physical process does.

chapters.applicability: General framework for thermoplastic moulded parts. Measurement conditioning and acceptance follow product/standard requirements.

sections.title: Dimensions can continue to change after ejection
sections.text: A moulded part is not necessarily dimensionally final when it leaves the mould. Continued cooling, residual-stress relaxation, crystallisation where applicable, moisture uptake or loss, and mechanical restraint can change measured dimensions over time.

sections.title: Define the reference condition before comparing parts
sections.text: Specify time after moulding, temperature, humidity or conditioning state, measurement equipment, datum scheme and operator method. Without a common reference condition, apparent process variation may actually be measurement-timing or conditioning variation.

sections.title: Separate moulding shrinkage from later dimensional movement
sections.text: Mould-to-part dimensional difference immediately after moulding and subsequent dimensional change are related but not identical questions. Track the dimension through time when the product requirement depends on delayed conditioning or stabilisation.

sections.title: Use direction and location as evidence
sections.text: Flow direction, transverse direction, fibre orientation, wall transitions, inserts, ribs and cooling layout can create anisotropic or local dimensional behavior. Mapping which dimensions move, in what direction and at what time helps distinguish global scale change from local distortion.

sections.title: Check the measurement system and fixture influence
sections.text: Contact force, fixturing, datum repeatability, part temperature and operator technique can contribute meaningful variation, especially for flexible or thin parts. Confirm the measurement method is capable before attributing small dimensional shifts to the moulding process.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Change the working diagnosis when the dimensional trend follows conditioning rather than process settings, differs by cavity or direction, disappears with improved measurement control, or persists after the suspected process variable is stabilised. The appropriate conclusion may be material-, tooling-, measurement- or product-design related rather than process-only.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General reinforced-thermoplastic behavior. Magnitude and property data are grade- and geometry-specific.

sections.title: Flow orients reinforcement
sections.text: Short fibres tend to develop orientation distributions as the melt shears and turns through the flow path; the distribution varies through thickness and around features.

sections.title: Orientation creates anisotropy
sections.text: Shrinkage, stiffness and strength can differ by direction, so reinforced parts may warp or perform differently from unfilled materials even with the same nominal geometry.

sections.title: Process and design interact
sections.text: Gate location, flow path, wall transitions and filling conditions can alter orientation. Use grade data and, where needed, simulation or measurement rather than generic shrinkage factors.

sections.title: Orientation connects flow history to directional properties
sections.text: Reinforcing fibres tend to develop orientation patterns influenced by local flow, geometry and the through-thickness velocity field. The resulting part can shrink, stiffen and distort differently by direction. A single nominal material property therefore cannot represent every local direction in a complex moulding.

sections.title: Infer carefully and measure where it matters
sections.text: Flow direction and geometry can suggest likely orientation, but they do not uniquely determine the final distribution. Dimensional vectors, mechanical testing, microscopy or validated simulation may be needed when orientation is critical. Treat orientation-based explanations as hypotheses until the evidence matches the required decision.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Conceptual guidance only. High-rate processing must remain within the actual machine, mould, material and hot-runner limits.

sections.title: Thin sections increase flow challenge
sections.text: Small flow thickness increases sensitivity to thermal loss and flow resistance, often requiring the system to deliver material quickly and repeatably.

sections.title: Machine capability matters
sections.text: Available injection rate, pressure, acceleration, control response and shot-size suitability can become limiting. A nominal pressure rating alone does not prove capability.

sections.title: Avoid universal high-speed rules
sections.text: Required rate depends on polymer rheology, geometry, gate and thermal condition. Establish it experimentally within supplier and equipment limits.

sections.title: Thin sections compress the available process window
sections.text: As flow paths become thinner relative to their length, pressure demand, cooling rate and sensitivity to small changes can increase. The process may have less tolerance for material, thermal, venting and machine-delivery variation. This makes measurement of actual machine response and mould behaviour especially important.

sections.title: Machine capability must be demonstrated, not assumed
sections.text: A high commanded velocity or pressure limit does not prove the machine can deliver the required profile through the actual mould. Review achievable velocity, acceleration, pressure response, transfer repeatability, shot utilisation and relevant equipment limits with the real system. Thin-wall processing should not be reduced to a generic instruction to run faster or hotter.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General balance methodology. Cavity layout, runner system and acceptance criteria are mould-specific.

sections.title: Equal nominal geometry does not guarantee equal cavity behavior
sections.text: Small differences in runner resistance, gate geometry or wear, venting, cavity temperature, cooling, local pressure transmission and mould construction can create systematic cavity-to-cavity variation even when cavities were designed to be identical.

sections.title: Preserve cavity identity in the data
sections.text: Record part mass, critical dimensions, defects and useful process signals by cavity. Pooling all parts into one average can hide one biased or unstable cavity and can make a balanced process appear noisier than it really is.

sections.title: Separate static imbalance from dynamic instability
sections.text: A cavity that is consistently heavier or fills earlier suggests a repeatable bias; a cavity that alternates or drifts suggests a different mechanism. Review both cavity means and time behavior before deciding whether the problem is runner/gate balance, thermal behavior, venting, measurement or another cause.

sections.title: Compare at equivalent process states
sections.text: Balance studies should control material condition, machine warm-up, mould thermal state, transfer method and sampling sequence. Otherwise time drift can be mistaken for cavity difference, particularly when cavities are measured in a fixed order.

sections.title: Tooling changes need stronger evidence than process compensation
sections.text: Changing a gate, runner or cavity feature can permanently alter the mould. Before modifying steel, demonstrate that the observed imbalance is repeatable, cavity-specific and not adequately explained by measurement, contamination, vent condition, thermal imbalance or process instability.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Reconsider a cavity-balance diagnosis when the bias changes sides with measurement order, disappears after thermal stabilisation or cleaning, follows a material or machine change, or is not repeatable across runs. Escalate unresolved imbalance with cavity-resolved evidence rather than masking it with a global setting change.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Source-first framework only. Processing windows, drying, residence and equipment requirements are grade-specific.

sections.title: The label does not define a process
sections.text: High-performance polymer families can differ greatly in melt temperature, moisture sensitivity, chemical compatibility and thermal stability.

sections.title: Use grade documents as controlling evidence
sections.text: Obtain the current TDS/processing guide/SDS for the exact grade and verify machine, screw, barrel, nozzle, mould and ancillary equipment compatibility.

sections.title: Thermal margin may be narrow
sections.text: When a material requires elevated processing temperature, actual melt history and residence distribution matter. Never substitute a generic family setting for the supplier's current requirements.

sections.title: High temperature increases the importance of system limits
sections.text: High-performance polymers can require processing conditions that place greater demands on dryers, barrel/nozzle capability, hot runners, mould temperature control, seals and safe handling. Generic family knowledge is not enough to define those conditions. Current grade and equipment documentation must establish the permitted window.

sections.title: Material change can change equipment compatibility
sections.text: A machine or hot-runner configuration suitable for one polymer may not be suitable for another because temperature capability, residence sensitivity, corrosion, wear, shear and purge requirements can differ. Treat a high-performance material introduction as a system-compatibility review rather than only a recipe change.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General advanced diagnostic method; production and safety decisions remain governed by site authority.

sections.title: Several mechanisms can fit the same symptom
sections.text: Advanced troubleshooting begins by accepting that one symptom can have several plausible causes. Dimensional drift, for example, may be consistent with material condition, thermal drift, packing response, cooling, measurement timing, cavity effects or tooling condition.

sections.title: Create competing hypotheses with predicted observations
sections.text: For each plausible mechanism, write down what else should be true if that mechanism is important: where the defect should occur, which cavities should be affected, how it should change with time, which signal should move, and which controlled comparison should alter the outcome.

sections.title: Prioritise discriminating evidence
sections.text: Choose observations or experiments that produce different predictions for the leading hypotheses. A test that improves the part but is consistent with every hypothesis has low diagnostic value; a test that separates two plausible causes can be more informative even if it does not immediately fix production.

sections.title: Use chronology and boundaries
sections.text: Ask what changed before the symptom appeared and define whether the effect is tied to a material lot, machine, mould, cavity, shift, maintenance event or environmental condition. Temporal and population boundaries often reduce the search space more effectively than changing several process settings.

sections.title: Beware of correlated signals and successful-but-wrong fixes
sections.text: Two variables can move together because both respond to a third mechanism. Likewise, a process change may suppress a symptom without correcting the underlying cause. Treat correlation and temporary improvement as evidence, not proof of causation.

sections.title: Preserve an evidence ledger
sections.text: Record the hypothesis, observation, test, predicted outcome, actual result and resulting confidence. This prevents repeated experiments, makes handover defensible and exposes when a conclusion rests on assumption rather than measurement.

sections.title: What evidence should change the conclusion?
sections.text: Reduce confidence when a prediction fails, the effect cannot be repeated, the symptom crosses the supposed boundary, or new evidence supports an alternative mechanism. When available evidence cannot discriminate among causes, document the unresolved set and hold the root-cause claim rather than inventing certainty.
